source: Ericsson, Krampe, Tesch-Romer (1993) The role of deliberate practice in the acquisition of expert performance
finding: Founding theory. Expert performance is the end result of long efforts to improve, called deliberate practice: tasks set by a teacher, a clear goal, immediate feedback, high effort, not enjoyable in itself. The authors say this gives a sufficient account of exceptional performance and reject any big role for innate talent, except body size.
numbers: Claims: individual differences even among elite performers are closely related to assessed deliberate practice; a minimum of about 10 years of effortful practice; the paper had over 9000 citations by 2018.
quote: Our theoretical framework can also provide a sufficient account of the major facts about the nature and scarcity of exceptional performance
limits: Retrospective interviews, small groups (10 per group), extreme-group designs. Wording moves between 'necessary' and 'sufficient'.
agent_relevance: The theory is about improvement inside one person under feedback. It never claimed that more hours of anything raises a system.

source: Ericsson et al. (1993) Study 1, violinists at the West Berlin academy
finding: Three groups of 10 violin students (best, good, music-teacher track) gave practice estimates. The best and good groups practiced alone about 24 h per week in the diary week, versus 9.3 for the teacher group. Authors claimed 'complete correspondence' between skill level and accumulated practice alone.
numbers: Practice alone accumulated by age 18: best 7,410 h, good 5,301 h (F(1,27)=4.59, p<.05); best and good combined vs teachers 3,420 h (F(1,27)=11.86, p<.01). Diary week 24.3 h vs 9.3 h, F(1,27)=44.05, p<.001. Uninterrupted sessions of 1 to 1.5 h.
limits: N=30. Interviewers probably not blind to group. Two ANOVAs each dropped one group but used full degrees of freedom. No variances reported.
agent_relevance: The 1 to 1.5 h session length is the theory's own dose limit. A scaffold should cap one pass and spend budget on fresh feedback, not repeat the loop.

source: Ericsson et al. (1993) Study 2, pianists, and the power-law view
finding: Expert pianists versus amateurs. By age 18 experts had accumulated far more practice. The paper treats improvement as a power law of practice when feedback exists; without adequate feedback, improvement is minimal even for motivated people.
numbers: Practice accumulated by age 18: experts 7,606 h vs amateurs 1,606 h, F(1,22)=26.29, p<.001. Older and younger expert groups did not differ at age 18 (F(1,22)=1.74, p>.20).
limits: Extreme-groups design (experts vs amateurs) inflates correlations. Hambrick 2014 note the expert group alone spanned about 10,000 to 30,000 h at ages 20 to 31.
agent_relevance: The formal core is the power law of practice plus a feedback condition. Same shape as test-time scaling with a verifier: gains need a signal.

source: Ericsson et al. (1993) limits on practice dose
finding: Theory predicts limits on daily practice because effortful practice is bounded by recovery. Cited laboratory work shows essentially no benefit beyond 4 h per day and reduced benefit beyond 2 h.
numbers: Effortful sessions 1 to 1.5 h in diaries. Benefit flat past about 4 h/day.
limits: Draws on older motor-learning literature (Welford, Woodworth and Schlosberg).
agent_relevance: Diminishing returns per session. More loops past a point buy little.

source: Hambrick, Oswald, Altmann, Meinz, Gobet, Campitelli (2014) Deliberate practice: Is that all it takes to become an expert?
finding: Reanalysis of six chess studies and eight music studies with correction for measurement error. Deliberate practice explained about a third of reliable variance. Not nearly sufficient.
numbers: Chess: 6 studies, pooled N=533, uncorrected r=.33 (95% CI .25 to .40), corrected r=.39; average 34.0% of variance explained, 66.0% not. Music: 8 studies, average 29.9% explained, 70.1% not. Assumed practice reliability .80. At reliability .60, chess left 54.7% unexplained and music 60.4%.
limits: Correlational. Practice is retrospective. Reliability is assumed. Platz et al. dispute the variance framing and the study set.
agent_relevance: Even with a generous correction the process variable leaves two thirds of outcome variance to other causes. Do not assume more rounds of any process explain most of a gain.

source: Hambrick et al. (2014) chess studies in detail
finding: Per-study chess correlations are moderate to strong but vary. The range of practice inside one skill level is huge and the groups overlap.
numbers: Corrected r: Charness 2005 Study 1 .63 (N=200), Study 2 .56 (N=164), Bilalic 2007 .49 (N=90 in table), de Bruin 2008 .81 (N=23), Howard 2012 .53 (N=73). Gobet and Campitelli 2007 (N=90): master 10,530 h (SD 7,414), expert 5,673 h (SD 4,654), intermediate 3,179 h (SD 4,615). Masters ranged 832 to 24,284 h; 5 of 16 masters (31.3%) had less practice than the expert-group mean.
limits: Grabner et al. 2007 (N=90, r=.08) excluded because practice only covered the current year.
agent_relevance: The same skill was reached with about 30 times different hours. Hours is a poor budget unit for an agent too.

source: Hambrick et al. (2014) music studies and other factors
finding: Eight music studies, corrected r from .30 to .75. Working memory capacity added unique variance beyond practice in sight-reading and did not interact with practice level. Starting age had effects on chess rating that were not mediated by practice.
numbers: Meinz and Hambrick (2010, N=57): practice explained 45.1% of sight-reading variance, working memory capacity another 7.4%; practice and working memory correlated r=.003. Corrected r by study: Lehmann and Ericsson 1996 .43 (N=16), Meinz 2000 .47 (N=107), Tuffiash 2002 .73 (N=135), Kopiez and Lee 2008 .30 (N=52), Ruthsatz 2008 .43/.39/.68, Meinz and Hambrick 2010 .75.
limits: Several small samples. Ericsson regards working memory as itself acquired.
agent_relevance: Capacity (working memory, context) and practice are separate and additive. A bigger buffer helps at any amount of rehearsal.

source: Hambrick et al. (2014) the attenuation-correction model
finding: The formal model is classical disattenuation: true r = observed r / sqrt(rxx * ryy). Practice reliability was assumed .80; chess rating reliability .91 from tournament outcome correlations.
numbers: Retrospective vs diary practice r: .74 (Ericsson 1993), .60 (de Bruin 2008), .98 to .99 (Bilalic 2007). Chess rating vs outcome r .93 to .96 (Olympiads), .83 to .93 (European Championship).
limits: Assumed reliabilities. Platz et al. object to squaring a corrected r.
agent_relevance: Any claim about the efficiency of an agent loop needs its own measured reliability, since noise hides gains.

source: Macnamara, Hambrick, Oswald (2014) Deliberate practice and performance in music, games, sports, education, and professions: a meta-analysis
finding: 88 studies from over 11,000 articles screened. Deliberate practice explained a sizeable but not majority share of performance variance, and the share fell in less structured domains. Original text gave games 26%, music 21%, sports 18%, education 4%, professions under 1% (12% overall); a 2018 corrigendum revised these.
numbers: Original (as in the subfield table; not opened this session): 26/21/18/4/<1, overall 12%. Corrigendum values quoted in Hambrick, Macnamara, Oswald 2020: overall 14%, games 24%, music 23%, sports 20%, education 5%, professions 1%.
limits: Not opened directly. Ericsson (2014) rejected 87 of the 88 studies as not meeting his definition. The practice measure included group and coached activity.
agent_relevance: The effect shrinks in domains with unstable rules, like most open-ended agent work. Practice pays most in closed, rule-stable games.

source: Hambrick, Macnamara, Oswald (2020) Is the deliberate practice view defensible?
finding: The authors restate their 2014 and 2016 results and reply to Ericsson. They show that conclusions swing with the assumed reliabilities, and argue Ericsson shifted the definition of deliberate practice to reject 87 of 88 studies, including some of his own.
numbers: Corrigendum numbers: 14% overall; games 24%, music 23%, sports 20%, education 5%, professions 1%. Sports meta-analysis: elite athletes 1%. A corrected r of .42 means 18% of variance.
limits: Authors are the original critics.
agent_relevance: The dispute is about definitions and reliability, not raw data. Define a good practice episode (goal, feedback, target) before counting it.

source: Hambrick et al. (2020) sensitivity table on Ericsson and Harwell's correlation
finding: Same data, very different variance shares depending on assumed reliability.
numbers: Using r=.56 for deliberate practice: reliabilities .60/.60 give corrected r=.93 (87.1%); .80/.80 give .70 (49.0%); .90/.90 give .62 (38.7%). With r=.54: .80/.80 gives .68 (45.6%).
limits: Sensitivity analysis, not new data.
agent_relevance: Report ranges, not single figures.

source: Macnamara, Moreau, Hambrick (2016) The relationship between deliberate practice and performance in sports: a meta-analysis
finding: Sports meta-analysis (abstract read through Europe PMC, plus Hambrick 2020). Deliberate practice explained 18% of variance overall, but only 1% among elite performers. Athletes who reached high skill did not start earlier than lower-skill athletes.
numbers: Overall 18% of variance; elite level (national and above) 1%. Solitary and group practice gave very similar effects.
limits: Range restriction at the elite level lowers r. Ericsson (2016) argues that summing any type of practice hours is the wrong measure.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: practice dose predicts level across wide ranges but not rank among the already best.

source: Ericsson (2016) Summing up hours of any type of practice versus identifying optimal practice activities
finding: Reply to the sports meta-analysis. It sums any sport-specific activity, including group activity, watching games on TV and play, which assumes all hours count the same. Calls for objective representative performance measures and longitudinal description.
numbers: No numbers (abstract only, via Europe PMC).
limits: Abstract-level reading.
agent_relevance: Quality of practice, not hours, is the real variable. Loop count is a poor proxy for useful feedback.

source: Macnamara and Maitra (2019) The role of deliberate practice in expert performance: revisiting Ericsson, Krampe and Tesch-Romer (1993)
finding: Double-blind replication of the violin study. The core finding was not replicated: the best violinists did not have more accumulated practice alone than the good violinists. Effect still substantial but smaller than the original.
numbers: Practice alone by age 18: best M=8,224 (95% CI 6,400 to 10,048), good M=9,844 (6,937 to 12,751), less accomplished M=4,558. Best vs good t(24)=-0.93, p=.364, d=-0.38; good vs less accomplished t(16.57)=3.26, p=.005, d=1.33. Group effect eta^2=.26 (95% CI .03 to .44). Original effect r=.70 versus the meta-analytic music average .48 (CI .38 to .56). Both top groups passed 10,000 h by age 20.
limits: About 13 violinists per group (F(2,36)). Kruskal-Wallis and Welch tests. Violinists started younger (about 5.5 vs 7.9 years).
agent_relevance: A failed replication of the best-known evidence. Treat single small studies on practice amounts as weak.

source: Macnamara and Maitra (2019) teacher-designed practice
finding: Tested the theoretical definition (teacher-designed practice) against the operational one (practice alone). Teacher-designed practice was rated less relevant to improvement and explained no more variance.
numbers: Teacher-designed practice by 18: best 6,251 h, good 6,821 h, less accomplished 2,799 h; chi2(2)=10.74, p=.005, eta^2=.23; best vs good d=-0.15; good vs less accomplished d=1.28. Practice alone and teacher-designed correlated r(37)=.72.
limits: Same small sample. Ericsson (2021) argues the definition is individualized teacher-led work, not measured time.
agent_relevance: If the teacher part adds no variance in humans, a stronger feedback source is not proven to be the active ingredient.

source: Platz, Kopiez, Lehmann, Wolf (2014) The influence of deliberate practice on musical achievement: a meta-analysis
finding: 13 music studies, N=788. The corrected aggregated correlation between accumulated task-relevant practice and music achievement was r_c=0.61 (95% CI 0.54 to 0.67), higher than Hambrick's .52. The authors say a variance framing is wrong and the result corroborates a central role of practice.
numbers: r_c=0.61, CI [0.54, 0.67]. Reanalysis of Hambrick's 8 studies uncorrected: r=0.44, I^2=60.3%, Q(7)=17.7, p<.02. Funnel plot nearly symmetric. Used practice to age 18 where possible (Kopiez and Lee r=.36 vs .25).
limits: Practice measures include non-deliberate parts. 0.61 squared is 37% of variance, leaving 63%.
agent_relevance: Same data, two readings: central role versus a third of variance. Quote both.

source: Hambrick, Altmann, Oswald, Meinz, Gobet (2014) Facing facts about deliberate practice
finding: Reply to Platz. Their 0.61 still leaves most variance to other factors; variance accounted for was used by Ericsson himself and by two Platz authors.
numbers: Restates: practice explained about one third of reliable variance in each domain; Platz r_c=0.61 vs own 0.52 (CI .43 to .64).
limits: Written by the original authors.
agent_relevance: Pair every correlation with its variance share before drawing a rule.

source: Ericsson and Harwell (2019) Deliberate practice and proposed limits on the effects of practice
finding: Reanalysis of Macnamara 2014 keeping only effects meeting three criteria for purposeful/deliberate practice. Accumulated practice explained about 29% of variance (61% after the authors' attenuation correction). Argues genetic effects are small except height and body size.
numbers: Random-effects r=.54 (95% CI .44 to .63), about 29% of variance, versus 14% in Macnamara 2014. Objective performance r=.49, relative performance r=.65. Per Hambrick 2020: r purposeful .51, deliberate .56.
limits: Selection of effects by the theory's author. Corrected share swings 49% to 87% with assumed reliability.
agent_relevance: A narrow definition of structured practice roughly doubles variance explained. Quality of feedback matters, time spent does not.

source: Ericsson (2021) Response to Macnamara and Hambrick (2020)
finding: Ericsson lists five criteria that define deliberate practice, with quotes from the 1993 paper, and says Macnamara et al. broadened it to lectures, student study alone and coach-led group activity. Offers a reconciliation proposal.
numbers: No new data. Five defining criteria.
limits: Argument paper, written in reply to a Scrabble commentary (Moxley, Ericsson, Tuffiash 2017).
agent_relevance: The theory cannot be tested by hours alone. Any test on an agent must pre-register what counts as deliberate.

source: Mosing, Verweij, Hambrick, Pedersen, Ullen (2024) Does practice reduce the heritability of musical expertise?
finding: Twin test of a direct prediction of the theory: genetic effects should shrink with more practice. They did not. Heritability rose with practice.
numbers: 6,471 twins (1,302 complete pairs), mean age 40.7. About 50% of musical expertise variance genetic, shared environment about 25%, residual about 25%. Practice-expertise r=0.36. Players vs non-players d=0.77 (males), 0.78 (females). With more practice shared and residual variance fell, genetic variance stayed flat.
limits: Expertise measured by auditory discrimination, not performance; practice in range categories.
agent_relevance: Practice shrinks noise but not the stable component. For agents the stable component is the base model.

source: Bilalic, McLeod, Gobet (2007) Does chess need intelligence? A study with young chess players
finding: 57 young players and an elite subsample of 23. Practice had the most influence on chess skill but intelligence added variance. In the elite children IQ correlated negatively with rating, because higher-IQ children practiced less.
numbers: Elite n=23: IQ and rating r(23)=-.51, p=.014; practice and rating r(23)=.46, p=.028. Model with practice explained 60% of rating variance, 30 points more than age and IQ alone; full model with experience 70%. Elite mean IQ 133 vs 114 in the rest.
limits: Small N. Selection into elite training may explain the negative sign.
agent_relevance: Ability and practice trade off. A stronger base model needs fewer scaffold rounds.

source: Burgoyne, Sala, Gobet, Macnamara, Campitelli, Hambrick (2016) Cognitive ability and chess skill: a meta-analysis
finding: Chess skill correlates with fluid reasoning, knowledge, short-term memory and speed at about r=.24 each, more in youth and at lower skill levels.
numbers: Average r=.24. Gf r=.32 youth vs .11 adults; .32 unranked vs .14 ranked. Numerical r=.35, verbal .19, visuospatial .13.
limits: Range restriction at higher skill. Correlational.
agent_relevance: Competing explanation: general ability matters most early, specific knowledge later.

source: Hambrick et al. (2014) competing factors and the Polgar case
finding: Competing factors named: working memory capacity, IQ, starting age. Equal intense training gave unequal results in the Polgar sisters.
numbers: Ericsson 1992 young chess players mean performance IQ 129 (top third 131, bottom third 124). One sister peaked at 2735 with an estimated 59,904 h; the two grandmaster sisters had more practice at peak than eight top-ten grandmasters in Howard's sample (M=14,020.5 h, SD=7,373.96).
limits: Case data from biographies.
agent_relevance: Same training and same scaffold still produce spread across runs.

source: Song et al. (2026) Deliberate practice in the age of AI: AI-assisted practice and self-regulated learning in conservatory musicians
finding: Three-wave 16-week study of AI music practice apps. Greater AI engagement was associated with later self-regulation, which was associated with later instructor-rated performance. Authors say AI apps support the conditions for deliberate practice, not replace it, and results are associations only.
numbers: 512 of 600 conservatory students completed all three waves (85.3%).
limits: Observational, heterogeneous apps, self-report, no objective usage logs, no multilevel clustering.
agent_relevance: Weak evidence that AI feedback helps human practice. It says nothing about LLM agents practicing themselves.

source: He, Panigrahi, Lin, Arora (2025) Skill-Targeted Adaptive Training (STAT)
finding: An LLM analogue of targeted practice. A stronger teacher model finds the skills a student lacks and builds data around them. Plain SFT saturates on MATH; targeted training does not.
numbers: Gains up to 7.5% on MATH across Llama and Qwen models; 4.6% average gain on AIME24/25 and AMC23; adds gains on top of GRPO.
limits: Read from the arXiv abstract page only. Needs a stronger teacher, which is the 'teacher-designed practice' ingredient.
agent_relevance: Supports the narrow definition: targeted, teacher-diagnosed practice beats repeated generic practice.

source: Rao et al. (2025) APT: weakness case acquisition and iterative preference training
finding: Trains a model only on its own error cases plus a few similar samples; claims domain gains without loss of general capability.
numbers: No numbers in abstract. Models Llama-2 and Mistral-V0.3.
limits: Abstract-level read only.
agent_relevance: Error-focused practice is the LLM counterpart of deliberate practice and may limit forgetting.
